question: During his interview on the Brussels Playbook Podcast on 10 September 2026, EU Commissioner Jørgensen stated that housing is partly a matter of EU competence because certain aspects of it relate to the free movement of services – including through short-term lettings – and to the free movement of capital, due to investments in the property market.

However, this line of reasoning appears to stretch the division of competences under the Treaties considerably. After all, the free movement of services and capital cannot automatically mean that the Union acquires general competence over matters falling exclusively within national competence, simply because there are points of overlap with the freedom of movement within those areas of competence.
If that were true, any tradable good or service would fall within EU competence, irrespective of the division of competences under the Treaties in the area concerned. 1.

Does the Commission acknowledge that the existence of a cross-border aspect, such as short-term lettings or cross-border property investments, does not in itself entail general EU competence in the field of housing, and that measures relating to spatial planning, housing supply, rent control and social housing fall, in principle, within the competence of the Member States?
Can the Commission indicate where, in its view, the legal boundary lies between measures to protect the internal market and de facto harmonisation of national housing policy?

Which competences, which are not currently regulated at EU level, does the Commission intend to regulate in future under the guise of general provisions such as the free movement of services and capital?
